topics.title: Chapter 29 — Cache Organization
topics.summary: A cache stores copies of blocks from a larger addressable space. Its organization determines where a block may reside and how hardware recognizes whether the requested block is present. The following models use byte addresses and power-of-two sizes to make the arithmetic transparent. Real processors add details such as physical or virtual indexing choices, coherence states, replacement approximations, and multiple cache levels. Use the simplified models to understand mapping and conflicts, not to infer every detail of a particular CPU from a virtual address alone. [ R3 ]

topics.title: 29.1 Cache blocks
topics.summary: A block is the fixed-size unit transferred between levels in the model. If blocks contain 64 bytes, addresses 0 through 63 belong to block 0, and addresses 64 through 127 belong to block 1. The block number is address / block_size , rounded down. The within-block offset selects the requested byte after the correct block has been found. Fetching a block can benefit later accesses to any of its bytes.

topics.title: 29.2 Cache lines
topics.summary: A cache line is the cache storage associated with one block’s data and its identifying state. Informal usage often treats “block” and “line” as interchangeable, but distinguishing the transferred block from its cache-resident slot can clarify replacement. A line contains metadata as well as data: a tag, validity information, and potentially dirty and coherence state. Capacity specifications usually refer to data capacity rather than including every metadata bit.

topics.title: 29.3 Cache slots
topics.summary: A slot is a possible resident location for a block. A direct-mapped cache gives each block exactly one eligible slot. More associative organizations give a block several or all slots as candidates. Replacement selects among eligible resident lines, not among arbitrary locations that the indexing rule forbids. This distinction is why unused capacity in one set does not necessarily help a different set that is experiencing conflicts.

topics.title: 29.4 Cache sets
topics.summary: A set groups the eligible slots for a mapping. If a cache has S sets and E ways per set, it has S*E data-line slots. A block maps to one set and can occupy one of that set’s ways. A two-way cache does not mean two sets. It means two eligible line positions within each set. Keep set count, associativity, and line size separate when calculating capacity.

topics.title: 29.5 Tags
topics.summary: A tag identifies which of the many blocks mapping to a set occupies a particular valid line. After selecting the set, the cache compares the requested tag with the valid resident tags. A tag match without a valid line is not a hit. Other state can affect whether a request can proceed, especially for writes in a coherent system. The basic read-only model tracks validity and tag identity.

topics.title: 29.7 Direct-mapped caches
topics.summary: A direct-mapped cache has one way per set. Lookup and replacement are simple because each block has one possible location. topics.title: 29.8 Set-associative caches
topics.summary: An E -way set-associative cache permits up to E resident blocks in each set. Associativity reduces some conflicts at the cost of more lookup and replacement complexity. topics.title: 29.9 Fully associative caches
topics.summary: A fully associative cache allows a block to occupy any line slot. In the model, it has one set and as many ways as resident lines. This removes set-index conflicts but leaves finite capacity and replacement decisions. Fully associative models are useful reference points for classifying misses. They are not automatically practical implementations for large, low-latency hardware caches because searching and maintaining many candidate entries has costs.

topics.title: Worked example — Decomposing an address
topics.summary: Assume a 32-KiB data cache, 64-byte lines, and eight ways. The set count is: There are 6 offset bits and 6 set-index bits. For address 0x1234 , the offset is 0x34 (52), the set is 0x08 (8), and the tag is 0x1 . The block number is 0x48 , or 72; 72 mod 64 = 8 . Address 0x2234 has the same offset and set but tag 2. The two addresses can coexist in different ways of the same set. In a direct-mapped cache with the same 64 sets and line size, they would compete for one line position. Notice that holding set count fixed while changing associativity also changes total capacity; fair comparisons must state which dimensions remain fixed.
